Vassūpanāyikakkhandhaka (The Chapter on Entering the Rains Retreat)
1. The Authorization for Entering the Rains Retreat.
At that time, the Buddha, the Blessed One, was dwelling at Rājagaha in the Bamboo Grove, the Squirrels’ Feeding Place.
Now at that time, the Blessed One had not yet prescribed the rains retreat for the bhikkhus.
Then the bhikkhus went on walking tours during the winter, the summer, and the rainy season.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:

“How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, go on walking tours during the winter, the summer, and the rainy season, trampling green grass, harming one-sensed life, and bringing many small creatures to their destruction?”
"Indeed, these followers of other sects, whose Dhamma is poorly proclaimed, will settle and dwell for the rains retreat.
Indeed, even these birds, having made their nests at the tops of trees, will settle and dwell for the rains retreat.

But these recluses, the sons of the Sakyans, wander on tour during the winter, the summer, and the rains; they trample upon green grass, harm living beings with a single sense-faculty, and bring many small creatures to destruction."
The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and resenting [the situation].
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this occasion, addressed the monks:
“I allow you, monks, to enter upon the rains residence.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“When, then, should the rains residence be entered?”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to enter upon the rains residence during the rainy season.
Then it occurred to the monks:
“How many, indeed, are the times for entering the rains retreat?
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Bhikkhus, there are these two times for entering the rains retreat:”
The earlier and the later.
The earlier [observance] should be entered upon when the Āsāḷhī full moon has passed; the later [observance] should be entered upon when one month has passed from the Āsāḷhī full moon.
These, monks, are the two observances for the rains.”
2. The Prohibition Against Wandering During the Rains Retreat, etc.
Now at that time, the group of six monks, having entered the rains retreat, went wandering during the middle of the rains.
People likewise complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:

“How can these recluses, sons of the Sakyan, go wandering on tour during the winter, the summer, and the rainy season alike—trampling green grass, harming living beings with a single sense-faculty, and bringing many small creatures to destruction?
For even those followers of other sects whose teachings are poorly expounded remain settled and dwell for the rains retreat;
even these birds, having made nests at the tops of trees, remain settled and dwell for the rains retreat.”

"But these recluses, sons of the Sakyans, wander on tour during the winter, the summer, and the rains; they trample down green grass, harm living beings with a single sense-faculty, and bring many small creatures to destruction. The monks heard those people grumbling, complaining, and criticizing. Those monks who were of few desires... [and so forth]... they grumbled, complained, and criticized: [The Buddha said: "Is it true, monks, that the monks wander on tour during the winter, the summer, and the rains; that they trample down green grass, harm living beings with a single sense-faculty, and bring many small creatures to destruction? "It is true, Blessed One. The Blessed One rebuked them, saying: "Monks, it is not fitting, it is not proper, it is not worthy of a recluse, it is not becoming, it is not suitable, it is not allowable, it is not to be done. How can these foolish men wander on tour during the winter, the summer, and the rains; trample down green grass, harm living beings with a single sense-faculty, and bring many small creatures to destruction? Monks, this is a training rule for you: one should not wander on tour during the winter, the summer, or the rains. Whoever should wander on tour during the winter, the summer, or the rains, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "I allow you, monks, to go on tour except during the three months of the rains. And you should not go on tour within a radius of seven days' journey from the place where you have spent the rains. Whoever should go on tour within a radius of seven days' journey from the place where he has spent the rains, there is an offense of wrong-doing. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "I allow you, monks, to go on tour except during the three months of the rains. And you should not go on tour within a radius of seven days' journey from the place where you have spent the rains, unless there is a reason. And what is the reason? There is danger from kings, or danger from thieves, or danger from fire, or danger from water, or danger from human beings, or danger from non-human beings, or danger from creeping animals, or danger to life, or the monastery is being destroyed. This is the reason. Then the Blessed One addressed the monks: "I allow you, monks, to go on tour except during the three months of the rains. And you should not go on tour within a radius of seven days' journey from the place where you have spent the rains, unless there is a reason. And what is the reason? “How indeed can the group-of-six monks, having entered the rains residence, go wandering during the middle of the rains?
Then those monks reported this matter to the Blessed One.
… [as before] … Then the Blessed One, on this occasion and in this connection, having given a discourse on the Dhamma, addressed the monks:
“Monks, having entered the rains residence, one should not set out on a journey without having dwelt for either the first three months or the last three months.
Whoever should set out commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, the group of six monks did not wish to enter the rains residence.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“Monks, one must not fail to enter the rains residence.
Whoever does not enter it incurs an offense of wrong-doing.”
Now at that time, on the very day of the entry into the rains retreat, the group-of-six monks intentionally passed by their residence because they did not wish to enter the rains retreat.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, on the very day of the entry into the rains retreat, one who does not wish to enter the rains retreat must not intentionally pass by his residence.”
“Whoever should exceed this limit commits an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, King Seniya Bimbisāra of Magadha, wishing to postpone the rains retreat, sent a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
“If, venerable sirs, you would enter upon the rains retreat during the next bright fortnight.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to comply with the requests of kings,” he said. 3.
The Allowance for a Seven-Day Business.
Then the Blessed One, having stayed at Rājagaha for as long as he pleased, set out on a wandering tour toward Sāvatthī.
Traveling by stages on his tour, he arrived at Sāvatthī.
There, the Blessed One dwelt at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s monastery.
Now at that time, in the Kosala country, a lay follower named Udena had had a monastery built for the sake of the Saṅgha.
He sent a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
"May the venerable ones come; I wish to give gifts, to hear the Dhamma, and to see the monks."
The bhikkhus said this:
“Friends, it has been laid down by the Blessed One:
‘Having entered the rains residence, one should not set out on a journey without having dwelt for either the first three months or the last three months.’”
“Let the lay follower Udena wait until the monks have completed the rains residence;
they will return once they have finished the rains.
But if he has urgent business, let him establish his dwelling right there in the presence of the resident monks.”
The lay follower Udena complained, grumbled, and expressed his displeasure:
“How can it be that the venerable ones do not come when sent for by me?
For I am a donor, a benefactor, and one who attends upon the Saṅgha.”
The bhikkhus heard Udena the lay follower complaining, grumbling, and lamenting.
Then those bhikkhus reported this matter to the Blessed One.
Thereupon, the Blessed One, having given a discourse on the Dhamma with reference to this cause and this context, addressed the bhikkhus:
“I allow you, monks, to go when sent for on account of a seven-day business, but not if not sent for.

I allow you, monks, to go when sent for on account of a seven-day business by these seven: a monk, a nun, a trainee nun, a male novice, a female novice, a male lay follower, or a female lay follower—but not if not sent for.”
A seven-day stay should be undertaken.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a lay follower has had a monastery built for the Saṅgha,
and he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks.

One must return within seven days.
Furthermore, bhikkhus, suppose a lay follower has had a hall built for the Saṅgha... [and so forth].”

Permission to Go Even When Not Invited for Five Reasons: “Monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business matter even when not invited if there are five reasons: (1) if one’s preceptor has fallen ill; (2) if one’s teacher has fallen ill; (3) if one’s fellow student has fallen ill;

(4) if one’s companion in the higher training has fallen ill; (5) if one wishes to ordain someone. Monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business matter even when not invited for these five reasons. One must return within seven days.”
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu was ill.
He sent a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying:
"I am ill; let the bhikkhus come, for I desire the arrival of the bhikkhus."
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to go for the sake of five kinds of business even if not invited, let alone if invited:
for a monk, for a nun, for a female trainee, for a male novice, or for a female novice.”
"I allow you, monks, to go for seven days on account of these five kinds of business even if not invited, let alone if invited.
A seven-day return must be made.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk is ill."
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
“I am ill; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day duty, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
“I will seek food for the sick, or seek food for the attendant of the sick, or seek medicine for the sick; or I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.”
A seven-day period of staying together should be observed.
Furthermore, monks, if dissatisfaction arises in a monk,
he might send a messenger to the presence of the other monks:

‘Discontent has arisen in me; let the bhikkhus come; I desire the coming of the bhikkhus,’ [if one says this], one may go on a seven-day mission even if not invited, much more so if invited—with the thought:
‘I will dispel his discontent, or have it dispelled for him, or I will give him a Dhamma talk.
One should remain away for seven days.
But here, monks, a monk has anxiety arise within him.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:

"Anxiety has arisen in me; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks," one may go, monks, on account of a matter to be done within seven days, even if not sent for, let alone if sent for.
‘I will dispel his remorse, or I will have it dispelled for him, or I will give him a discourse on the Dhamma.
In such a case, monks, a seven-day period of staying together must be observed. Furthermore, monks, there may arise in a monk a certain speculative view.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying, “A wrong view has arisen in me;
let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks,” then, monks, you may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
“I will resolve his wrong view, or have it resolved, or I will give him a discourse on the Dhamma.”
A seven-day period of suspension must be observed.
But here, monks, a monk has committed a grave offense (garudhamma) and is subject to probation.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

‘For I have committed a heavy offense and am deserving of probation; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks,’ [if one says this], one may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not sent for, let alone if sent for—with the thought:
‘I will make an effort to grant the probation, or I will make the proclamation, or I will be one who completes the quorum.
One should make a return within seven days.
But here, monks, a monk becomes one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:

"I am one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning; let the monks come, for I desire the coming of the monks," then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited.
‘I will make an effort for his restoration to the beginning, or I will announce [the formal act], or I will be one who completes the quorum.
For seven days, he should remain in retreat.
But here, monks, there is a monk who deserves the *mānatta* penance.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:

“I am deserving of the *mānatta* discipline; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks,” then, monks, one may go on account of a business to be done within seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
“I shall exert myself to grant the *mānatta* discipline, or I shall make the proclamation, or I shall be one who completes the quorum.”
A seven-day period of suspension must be observed.
But here, monks, there is a monk who is deserving of rehabilitation.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

‘I am worthy of rehabilitation; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks. In such a case, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business even if not invited, much more so if invited, thinking:
‘I will exert myself for his rehabilitation, or I will make the proclamation, or I will be one who completes the quorum.
One must return within seven days.
But here, monks, when a Saṅgha intends to carry out a formal act against a monk— whether it be one of censure, demotion, banishment, reconciliation, or suspension—
if he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks saying,

“The Saṅgha intends to carry out a formal act against me; let the monks come, for I desire the coming of the monks,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited.
‘How might the Saṅgha not perform a legal act against me, or how might it transform it into a lighter one?
He should remain in retreat for seven days.
Or, a legal act may have been performed against him by the Saṅgha—whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:

“The Saṅgha has performed a formal act against me; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks,” then, monks, one may go on account of a business to be done within seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
“How might he conduct himself properly, shed his hair, behave so as to reach resolution, and how might the Saṅgha cause that formal act to be pacified?”
A seven-day period of staying together should be observed.
But here, monks, if a bhikkhunī becomes ill and she should send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus:
‘I am ill; may the masters come, for I desire the masters’ coming,’ [if one says this,] monks, one may go on a seven-day mission even if not requested, let alone if requested—with the thought:
‘I will seek food for the sick, or seek food for the attendant of the sick, or seek medicine for the sick, or I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.
One must return within seven days.
"Furthermore, monks, if dissatisfaction has arisen in a bhikkhunī, and she should send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying: 'Dissatisfaction has arisen in me;
may the noble ones come; I desire the coming of the noble ones,' then, monks, one may go for seven days' business, even if not invited, let alone if invited."
‘I will cause her who is dissatisfied to be secluded, or I will have her secluded, or I will give her a discourse on the Dhamma.
A seven-day period of retreat must be observed.
But here, monks, a certain bhikkhunī has become anxious.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying, “Anxiety has arisen in me;
may the masters come, for I desire the masters’ arrival,” then, monks, one may go on account of a business to be done within seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
“I will dispel her anxiety, or I will have it dispelled for her, or I will give her a discourse on the Dhamma.”
A seven-day period of staying together must be observed.
Furthermore, monks, if a wrong view has arisen in a bhikkhunī, she may send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying: [“I have a certain matter; please come.”]

‘A view has arisen in me; let the noble ladies come, for I wish for the noble ladies to come. In such a case, monks, one may go on account of a business that must be done during seven days, even if not invited, much more so if invited—with the thought:
‘I will dispel this view myself, or have it dispelled, or I will give a Dhamma talk to her.
One should remain away for seven days.
But here, monks, a bhikkhunī has committed a grave offense (garudhamma) and is subject to the penance of *mānatta*.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying:

“I have indeed committed a grave offense and am subject to the *mānatta* penance; may the noble ones come, for I desire the coming of the noble ones,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited.
‘I will make an effort to grant the mānatta penance.
A seven-day period of staying together must be observed.
But here, monks, a bhikkhunī is subject to being sent back to the beginning.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:

“I am subject to being sent back to the beginning; may the venerable ones come, for I desire the coming of the venerable ones,” then, monks, one may go on account of a business matter lasting seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited, thinking:
“I will make an effort regarding her being sent back to the beginning.”
A seven-day period of suspension must be observed.
But here, monks, there may be a nun who is deserving of rehabilitation.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

‘I am worthy of rehabilitation; let the masters come, for I desire the masters’ coming,’ [if this is said], then, monks, one may go on a seven-day mission even if not invited, much more so if invited, thinking:
‘I shall make an effort toward his rehabilitation.
One should return within seven days.
But here, monks, a Sangha wishes to carry out a formal act against a bhikkhunī—
whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus:

‘The Saṅgha wishes to perform a formal act against me; let the venerable ones come, for I desire the venerable ones to come,’ [if this is said], monks, one may go on account of business for seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
‘How might the Saṅgha not perform the formal act, or perhaps transform it into a lighter one?
One must ensure that there is a return within seven days.
Or perhaps a formal legal act has been carried out against her by the Saṅgha—
whether it be a censure, a demotion, a banishment, a reconciliation, or a suspension.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

“If [the person] says, ‘The Saṅgha has performed a legal act against me; may the venerable ones come, for I desire the coming of the venerable ones,’ then, monks, one may go on account of business for seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
‘How might he conduct himself properly, grow his hair, conduct himself so as to reach a resolution, and cause the Saṅgha to suspend that legal act?
One should make a seven-day return.”
But here, monks, a trainee nun (sikkhamānā) becomes ill.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
“I am ill; may the venerable ones come; I desire the venerable ones to come,” then, monks, one may go for the sake of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited.
‘I will seek out food for the sick, or I will seek out food for the attendant of the sick, or I will seek out medicine for the sick; I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.
A seven-day period of absence may be taken.
But here, monks, if dissatisfaction has arisen in a female trainee (sikkhamānā) … [as before] …”
Remorse arises in a trainee nun...
a speculative view arises in a trainee nun...
the training is violated by a trainee nun.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying, “My training has been interrupted;
may the masters come, for I desire the masters’ arrival,” then, monks, one may go on account of a business that must be done within seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited, thinking:
“I shall make an effort toward the undertaking of the training.”
A seven-day stay should be arranged.
But here, monks, there may be a trainee nun who wishes to receive full ordination.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

‘For I desire to grant full ordination; let the noble ladies come, for I wish for the noble ladies to come’—if this is said, monks, one may go on a seven-day mission even if not invited, much more so if invited, thinking:
‘I will make an effort regarding the full ordination, or I will perform the proclamation, or I will be the one who completes the quorum.
One must return within seven days.
But here, monks, a novice is ill.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
"I am ill; let the monks come, for I desire the arrival of the monks," then, monks, one may go on account of that seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited.
‘I will seek food for the sick, or I will seek food for the attendant of the sick, or I will seek medicine for the sick; I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.
A seven-day period of absence may be granted.
But here, monks, if dissatisfaction arises in a novice... [and so on].
A novice monk becomes anxious;
a novice monk develops a wrong view;
a novice monk desires to ask about the rains-residence.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the bhikkhus, saying:

“I wish to ask about the rains; let the bhikkhus come, for I desire the arrival of the bhikkhus,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day task even if not invited, how much more so if invited, thinking:
“I will ask him, or I will explain [the matter] to him.”
A seven-day stay should be arranged.
Furthermore, monks, suppose there is a novice who wishes to receive full ordination.
If he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

‘For I wish to receive full ordination; let the bhikkhus come; I desire the arrival of the bhikkhus’—if this is said, bhikkhus, one may go on account of a seven-day task even if not invited, how much more so if invited, thinking:
‘I will make an effort for the full ordination, or I will perform the proclamation, or I will be one who completes the quorum.
One must ensure a return within seven days.
But here, monks, a novice nun may be ill.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
"I am ill; let the venerable ones come, for I desire the venerable ones to come," then, monks, one may go on account of that seven-day business, even if not sent for, let alone if sent for.
‘I will seek food for the sick, or I will seek food for the attendant of the sick, or I will seek medicine for the sick; I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.
In such a case, a seven-day period of absence may be granted.
Furthermore, monks, it may happen that dissatisfaction arises in a female novice... [and so forth].
A novice nun becomes anxious;
a novice nun develops a wrong view;
a novice nun wishes to ask about the rains residence.
If she should send a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying, “I wish to ask about the rains;
let the venerable ones come, for I desire the coming of the venerable ones,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited, thinking:
“I shall ask her, or I shall give her instruction.”
A seven-day period of residence must be observed.
Furthermore, monks, if a female novice (sāmaṇerī) wishes to undertake the training and should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:

“If [a woman says], ‘I wish to undertake the training; let the noble ladies come, for I desire the coming of the noble ladies,’ then, monks, one may go on account of a business that must be done within seven days, even if not invited, let alone if invited, thinking:
‘I will make an effort to have her undertake the training.
A seven-day period of absence should be observed.”
5. Permission Even for Those Not Requested.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu’s mother was ill.
She sent a messenger to her son, saying: [text continues]
“I am ill; let my son come, for I desire the arrival of my son.
Then it occurred to that bhikkhu:
“It has been laid down by the Blessed One—”
"One may go when sent for on seven kinds of business that require a seven-day period, but not if not sent for;
one may go even if not sent for on five kinds of business that require a seven-day period, let alone if sent for.
Now my mother is ill, yet she is not a lay follower; how indeed should I proceed?"
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to go for seven days on account of a duty, even if not invited, let alone if invited:
[for the sake of] a monk, a nun, a female trainee, a male novice, a female novice, and for one’s mother and father.”
"I allow you, monks, to go for seven days on account of these seven kinds of business, even if not sent for, let alone if sent for.
A seven-day period must be observed.
Now, monks, suppose a monk’s mother is ill."
If she should send a messenger to her son, saying:
“I am ill; let my son come, for I desire my son’s arrival,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business, even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
“I will seek food for the sick, or seek food for the attendant of the sick, or seek medicine for the sick, or I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.”
A seven-day period of absence may be taken.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk’s father is ill;
he might send a messenger to his son, saying: [text continues]
‘I am ill; let my son come, for I desire my son’s arrival. In such a case, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day task even if not invited, let alone if invited—with the thought:
‘I will seek food for the sick, or seek food for the attendant of the sick, or seek medicine for the sick; or I will inquire after him, or I will attend to him.
One must return within seven days.
6. Sending a messenger for permission:
Now, monks, suppose a monk’s brother is ill.
He might send a messenger to his brother, saying: [“Please come.”]
‘I am ill; let my brother come, for I desire my brother’s arrival. In such a case, monks, one may go on a seven-day mission if sent for, but not if not sent for.
One must return within seven days.
Furthermore, monks, suppose a monk’s sister is ill.
If she should send a messenger to her brother, saying:
“I am ill; let my brother come, for I desire my brother’s arrival,” then, monks, one may go on account of a seven-day business when so sent, but not if not so sent.
A seven-day stay must be observed.
But here, monks, a relative of a monk falls ill. If he should send a messenger to the presence of that monk, saying, “I am indeed ill;
may the venerable one come, for I desire the venerable one’s arrival,” then, monks, one may go on account of this seven-day business when so sent for, but not if not so sent for.
A seven-day period of staying together should be observed.
Furthermore, monks, suppose there is a monk who is traveling and he falls ill;
if he should send a messenger to the presence of the monks:
‘“I am ill; let the venerable ones come; I desire the venerable ones’ coming,” [if one says this], monks, one may go on account of a seven-day task when sent for, but not if not sent for.
A seven-day return must be made.
Now at that time, the Saṅgha’s dwelling was falling into decay.
A certain lay follower had timber cut in the forest.
He sent a messenger to the presence of the monks, saying:
“If the venerable sirs would have that timber brought here, I would give it to them.”
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to go on business for the Saṅgha.
A seven-day period of absence must be observed.”
The section on the rains residence is finished.
7. The section on non-offenses regarding interruptions to the rains residence due to obstacles:
Now at that time, in a certain monastery in the Kosala country, the monks who had entered the rains residence were harassed by wild beasts.
They seized them and even beat them.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One:
“In this case, monks, monks who have entered the rains residence are harassed by wild beasts.”
They seize them or cause them to fall;
this is indeed an obstacle, so one must depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat.
But here, monks, when monks who have entered the rains residence are harassed by reptiles—
which bite them and even carry them off—
they may depart, thinking: "This is indeed an obstacle."
There is no offense in interrupting the rains residence.
Furthermore, monks, there may be cases where monks who have entered the rains residence are harassed by bandits;
they plunder them and even beat them.
"This itself is an obstacle," [thinking thus,] one may depart.
There is no offense for interrupting the rains residence.
Furthermore, monks, in this case, the monks who have entered the rains residence are harassed by malevolent spirits (pisāca).
They may even enter [the body] or kill [the person].
"This indeed is an obstacle," thinking thus, one should depart.
There is no offense in interrupting the rains residence.
But here, monks, when monks have entered the rains residence, their village is burned by fire.
The monks are distressed for lack of almsfood.
Thinking, "This indeed is an obstacle," they may depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
But here, monks, when the lodgings of monks who have entered the rains residence have been burnt by fire,
the monks are distressed for lack of lodgings.
"This very thing constitutes an obstacle; one should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat.
Furthermore, monks, it may happen that while the monks have entered the rains-retreat, their village is swept away by water."
The bhikkhus were exhausted by their lack of almsfood.
[Thinking], "This indeed is an obstacle," they should depart.
There is no offense in interrupting the rains residence.
But here, monks, when the lodgings of monks who have entered the rains residence have been swept away by water,
and the monks are distressed by the lodgings,
they may depart, thinking: "This indeed is an obstacle."
“There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
Now at that time, in a certain monastery, the village of the monks who had entered the rains residence was plundered by bandits.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to go toward whichever village is [near].
A village was split into two factions.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, monks, to go where there are more [of those who are faithful].
There were more who were faithless and lacked confidence.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to go wherever those who have faith and confidence reside.

Now at that time, in a certain monastery in the Kosala country, monks who had entered the rains retreat were unable to obtain as much coarse or refined food as they required for their full satisfaction.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.

“Furthermore, monks, when monks who have entered the rains residence do not obtain, to their heart’s content and full satisfaction, either coarse or refined food, this indeed is an obstacle; they may depart.
There is no offense for breaking the rains residence.”
But here, monks, when monks who have entered the rains residence obtain as much of coarse or refined food as they require for their full satisfaction, yet do not obtain suitable food— thinking,
"This is indeed an obstacle," they may depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.

But here, monks, when monks who have entered the rains residence obtain as much as they need for their full satisfaction of food, whether coarse or refined, and obtain suitable foods, yet do not obtain suitable medicines—this indeed is an obstacle; one may depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
But here, monks, monks who have entered the rains residence obtain as much of coarse or refined food as they require for their full satisfaction;
they obtain suitable foods; they obtain suitable medicines;
yet they do not obtain a suitable attendant.
Thinking, "This indeed is an obstacle," one should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat.
But here, monks, a woman invites a monk who has entered the rains-retreat:
“Come, venerable sir, I will give you gold, or I will give you silver, or I will give you a field,
or I will give you a site, or I will give you a bull, or I will give you a cow, or I will give you a male slave, or I will give you a female slave,
or I will give you my daughter for the sake of a wife; or I myself will become your wife, or I will bring another wife for you.”
In that case, if it occurs to a bhikkhu:
“The Blessed One has said that the mind turns quickly; there might be an obstacle to my holy life,” he should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
But here, monks, a courtesan invites a monk who has entered the rains residence … a grown-up virgin invites him … a paṇḍaka invites him … [and so on].
Relatives invite them...
kings invite them...
thieves invite them...
The scoundrels invited him, saying:

“Come, venerable sir! We will give you gold coin, or we will give you gold, or we will give you a field, or we will give you a building site, or we will give you a bull, or we will give you a cow, or we will give you a male slave, or we will give you a female slave.”
‘We will give you our daughter for the sake of being your wife, or we will bring another wife for you.
If, in that situation, it occurs to the bhikkhu:
‘The mind is said by the Blessed One to be quick to change; there might even be an obstacle to my holy life,’ he should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains-retreat.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered the rains-retreat sees a treasure-trove that has no owner.
If it occurs to that monk:
‘The mind has been described by the Blessed One as quick to change; there might be an obstacle to my holy life,’ [thinking thus], he should depart.
There is no offense for interrupting the rains residence.
8. The Chapter on No Offense for Interrupting the Rains Residence Due to Schism in the Saṅgha.
"Furthermore, monks, here a monk who has entered the rains residence sees many monks striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.
If, in that situation, it occurs to the monk:
'A schism in the Saṅgha is indeed called grave by the Blessed One;'"
Thinking, "May the Saṅgha not split while I am present," one should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk who has entered the rains residence hears:
‘It is said that in such-and-such a residence many bhikkhus are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.
If, in that case, it occurs to a bhikkhu:
‘A schism in the Saṅgha has been declared by the Blessed One to be a grave matter;’
"If the Saṅgha should split while I am present, I shall depart.
There is no offense for breaking the rains-retreat.
Furthermore, monks, here a monk who has entered the rains-retreat hears:
‘It is said that in such-and-such a residence, a number of bhikkhus are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.
If, in this regard, it occurs to a bhikkhu:
‘Those bhikkhus are my friends.’
If he thinks, "I shall say to them, 'Friend, the schism in the Saṅgha has been called grave by the Blessed One;
may it not please the venerable ones to cause a schism in the Saṅgha,' and they will follow my word, they will listen, and they will lend an ear," then he should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains retreat.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered the rains retreat hears:
"It is said that in such-and-such a residence, several monks are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha."
In that case, if it occurs to a bhikkhu:
"Those bhikkhus are not my friends;
rather, those who are their friends are my friends."
I will say this to them.
When they have been told this, they will say: "Friend, the schism of the Saṅgha has been called grave by the Blessed One;
let not the schism of the Saṅgha be pleasing to you, venerable sirs."
‘They will act upon their words, they will listen, and they will lend an ear,’ one should depart.
There is no offense for breaking the rains residence.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered the rains residence hears:
‘It is said that in such-and-such a residence the Saṅgha has been split by a number of bhikkhus.
If, in this regard, it occurs to a bhikkhu:
‘Those bhikkhus are indeed my friends.’
Thinking, "I will say to them, 'Friend, the schism of the Saṅgha has been called grave by the Blessed One;
may the Venerable Ones not take pleasure in a schism of the Saṅgha,' and they will follow my word, they will listen, and they will lend an ear," one should depart.
There is no offense for interrupting the rains retreat.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered the rains retreat hears:
"It is said that in such-and-such a residence, the Saṅgha has been split by a number of monks."
In that case, if it occurs to a bhikkhu:
"Those bhikkhus are not my friends;
rather, those who are their friends are my friends."
I shall speak to them;
having been spoken to by me, they will say, "Friend, the schism of the Saṅgha has been called grave by the Blessed One;
may the venerable ones not take pleasure in a schism of the Saṅgha."
‘They will act upon their words, they will listen, and they will lend an ear,’ one should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered the rains residence hears:
‘It seems that in such-and-such a residence, a number of bhikkhunīs are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.
If it occurs to that bhikkhu:
‘Those bhikkhunīs are indeed my friends.’
Thinking, "I will say to them, 'Sisters, the schism of the Saṅgha has been called grave by the Blessed One;
may the schism of the Saṅgha not be pleasing to you,
sisters,' and they will follow my word, they will listen, and they will lend an ear," one should depart.
There is no offense in interrupting the rains residence.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered for the rains hears:
“It is said that in such-and-such a residence, many bhikkhunīs are striving for a schism in the Saṅgha.”
In that case, if a bhikkhu thinks:
"Those bhikkhunīs are not my friends;
rather, those who are their friends are my friends."
I shall speak to them;
having been spoken to, they will say: "Sisters, the schism of the Saṅgha has been declared by the Blessed One to be a grave matter.
Sisters, let the schism of the Saṅgha not be pleasing to you."
‘They will do as they are told, they will listen, and they will lend an ear,’ one may depart.
There is no offense regarding the interruption of the rains residence.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered the rains residence hears:
‘It is said that in such-and-such a residence the Saṅgha has been split by a number of bhikkhunīs.
If it occurs to that bhikkhu:
‘Those bhikkhunīs are indeed my friends.’
Thinking, "I shall say to them: 'Sisters, the schism of the Saṅgha has been called grave by the Blessed One.
May the schism of the Saṅgha not be pleasing to you,' and they will follow my word, they will listen, and they will lend an ear," one may depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
But here, monks, a monk who has entered for the rains hears:
"It is said that in such-and-such a residence, the Saṅgha has been split by a number of bhikkhunīs."
In that case, if it occurs to a bhikkhu:
"Those bhikkhunīs are not my friends;
rather, those who are their friends are my friends."
I shall speak to them.
When they have been spoken to, they will say: "Sisters, the schism of the Saṅgha has been declared by the Blessed One to be a grave matter;
may the schism of the Saṅgha not be pleasing to you, sisters."
"If they will act upon their words, listen to them, and lend an ear," one should depart.
There is no offense in breaking the rains residence.
9. Entering the Rains Residence in Vajjī and Other Places.
Now at that time, a certain monk wished to enter the rains residence during the month of Vaja.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to enter the rains residence during the month of Vaja.”
A storm arose.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, I allow you to go wherever there is a storm.”
Now at that time, as the commencement of the rains was approaching, a certain bhikkhu wished to travel with a caravan.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to enter upon the rains residence within a caravan,” he said.
Now at that time, a certain bhikkhu wished to travel by boat as the time for entering the rains retreat was approaching.
They reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“I allow you, bhikkhus, to enter the rains retreat on a boat,” he said.
10. Places Where One Should Not Enter for the Rains Retreat.
Now at that time, monks entered the rains retreat in hollow trees.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just like a little goblin,” they reported this matter to the Blessed One.
“Monks, one should not enter the rains residence in the hollow of a tree.”
“Whoever should enter the rains residence [there], there is an offense of wrong-doing.
Now at that time, monks entered the rains residence in the fork of a tree.
People complained, grumbled, and became indignant, saying:
“It is just as if they were deer-hunters.
